{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{Short description|Upper bound on the knowable information of a quantum state}}
'''Holevo's theorem''' is a result in [[quantum information theory]]. It is sometimes called '''Holevo's bound''', since it gives an [[upper bound]] on the accessible information, which is amount of information that can be known about a [[quantum state]]. It was first published by [[Alexander Holevo]] in 1973.

==Statement==
===Setting===
Suppose Alice wants to send a classical message to Bob by encoding it into a quantum state, and suppose she can prepare a state from some fixed set <math>\{\rho_1,...,\rho_n\}</math>, with the i-th state prepared with probability <math>p_i</math>. Let <math>X</math> be the classical register containing the choice of state made by Alice. Bob's objective is to recover the value of <math>X</math> by measuring a [[POVM]] on the state he received. Let <math>Y</math> be the classical register containing Bob's measurement outcome, which is a random variable whose distribution depends on Bob's choice of measurement.

Holevo's theorem bounds the amount of correlation between the classical registers <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, independently of Bob's measurement choice, in terms of the ''Holevo information''. The Holevo information does not depend on the measurement choice, and so this gives a bound which does not require optimizing over all possible measurements.

===Precise statement===
Define the ''accessible information'' between <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> as the (classical) mutual information between the two registers maximized over all possible choices of Bob's measurements:
<math display="block">I_{\rm acc}(X:Y) = \sup_{\{\Pi^B_i\}_i } I(X:Y|\{\Pi^B_i\}_i),</math>
where <math>I(X:Y|\{\Pi^B_i\}_i)</math> is the classical mutual information of the joint probability distribution given by <math>p_{ij} = p_i \operatorname{Tr}(\Pi^B_j \rho_i)</math>. There is no known formula for the accessible information in general. However, there is always an upper bound
<math display="block">I_{\rm acc} (X : Y) \leq \chi(\eta) \equiv  S\left(\sum_i p_i \rho_i\right) - \sum_i p_i S(\rho_i),</math>
where <math>\eta\equiv\{(p_i,\rho_i)\}_i</math> is the ensemble of states Alice uses to send information, and <math>S</math> is the [[von Neumann entropy]]. The quantity <math>\chi(\eta)</math> is called the '''Holevo information''' or '''Holevo ''χ'' quantity'''.

The Holevo information is also equal to the [[quantum mutual information]] of the classical-quantum state corresponding to the ensemble:<math display="block">\chi(\eta) = I\left(\sum_i p_i |i\rangle\!\langle i|\otimes \rho_i\right),</math>where <math>I(\rho_{AB}) \equiv S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B) - S(\rho_{AB})</math> the quantum mutual information of the bipartite state <math>\rho_{AB}</math>. Holevo's theorem can also be stated as a bound on the accessible information in terms of the quantum mutual information of a classical-quantum state.

==Proof==
Consider the composite system that describes the entire communication process, which involves Alice's classical input <math>X</math>, the quantum system <math>Q</math>, and Bob's classical output <math>Y</math>. The classical input <math>X</math> can be written as a classical register <math>\rho^X := \sum\nolimits_{x=1}^n p_x |x\rangle \langle x|</math> with respect to some orthonormal basis <math>\{|x\rangle\}_{x=1}^n</math>. By writing <math>X</math> in this manner, the [[von Neumann entropy]] <math>S(X)</math> of the state <math>\rho^X</math> corresponds to the [[Entropy (information theory)|Shannon entropy]] <math>H(X)</math> of the probability distribution <math>\{p_x\}_{x=1}^n</math>:
:<math>
S(X)
= -\operatorname{tr}\left(\rho^X \log \rho^X \right)
= -\operatorname{tr}\left(\sum_{x=1}^n  p_x \log p_x  |x\rangle\langle x|\right)
= -\sum_{x=1}^n p_x \log p_x
= H(X).
</math>

The initial state of the system, where Alice prepares the state <math>\rho_x</math> with probability <math>p_x</math>, is described by
:<math>\rho^{XQ} := \sum_{x=1}^n p_x |x\rangle \langle x|\otimes\rho_x.</math>

Afterwards, Alice sends the quantum state to Bob. As Bob only has access to the quantum system <math>Q</math> but not the input <math>X</math>, he receives a mixed state of the form <math>\rho := \operatorname{tr}_X\left(\rho^{XQ}\right) = \sum\nolimits_{x=1}^n p_x \rho_x</math>. Bob measures this state with respect to the [[POVM]] elements <math>\{E_y\}_{y=1}^m</math>, and the probabilities <math>\{q_y\}_{y=1}^m</math> of measuring the outcomes <math>y=1,2,\dots,m</math> form the classical output <math>Y</math>. This measurement process can be described as a [[quantum instrument]]
:<math>\mathcal{E}^{Q}(\rho_x) = \sum_{y=1}^m q_{y|x} \rho_{y|x} \otimes |y\rangle \langle y|,</math>
where <math>q_{y|x} = \operatorname{tr}\left(E_y\rho_x\right)</math> is the probability of outcome <math>y</math> given the state <math>\rho_x</math>, while <math>\rho_{y|x} = W\sqrt{E_y}\rho_x\sqrt{E_y}W^\dagger/q_{y|x}</math> for some unitary <math>W</math> is the normalised [[POVM#Post-measurement state|post-measurement state]]. Then, the state of the entire system after the measurement process is
:<math>\rho^{XQ'Y} := \left[\mathcal{I}^{X}\otimes\mathcal{E}^{Q}\right]\!\left(\rho^{XQ}\right) = \sum_{x=1}^n\sum_{y=1}^m  p_x q_{y|x} |x\rangle \langle x|\otimes\rho_{y|x}\otimes |y\rangle \langle y|.</math>

Here <math>\mathcal{I}^X</math> is the identity channel on the system <math>X</math>. Since <math>\mathcal{E}^Q</math> is a [[Quantum channel#Instrument|quantum channel]], and the [[quantum mutual information]] is monotonic under [[Completely positive map|completely positive]] trace-preserving maps,<ref name="Preskill">{{cite book |last=Preskill |first=John |author-link1=John Preskill |date=June 2016|title=Quantum Information |chapter=Chapter 10. Quantum Shannon Theory |chapter-url= https://authors.library.caltech.edu/66493/2/chap10_15.pdf |pages=23–24 |access-date= 30 June 2021}}</ref> <math>S(X:Q'Y) \leq S(X:Q)</math>. Additionally, as the [[partial trace]] over <math>Q'</math> is also completely positive and trace-preserving, <math>S(X:Y) \leq S(X:Q'Y)</math>. These two inequalities give
:<math>S(X:Y) \leq S(X:Q).</math>

On the left-hand side, the quantities of interest depend only on
:<math>\rho^{XY} := \operatorname{tr}_{Q'}\left(\rho^{XQ'Y}\right) = \sum_{x=1}^n\sum_{y=1}^m  p_x q_{y|x} |x\rangle \langle x|\otimes |y\rangle \langle y|
= \sum_{x=1}^n\sum_{y=1}^m  p_{x,y} |x,y\rangle \langle x,y|,</math>
with [[Joint probability distribution|joint probabilities]] <math>p_{x,y}=p_x q_{y|x}</math>. Clearly, <math>\rho^{XY}</math> and <math>\rho^Y := \operatorname{tr}_X(\rho^{XY})</math>, which are in the same form as <math>\rho^X</math>, describe classical registers. Hence,
:<math>S(X:Y) = S(X)+S(Y)-S(XY) = H(X)+H(Y)-H(XY) = I(X:Y).</math>

Meanwhile, <math>S(X:Q)</math> depends on the term
:<math>\log \rho^{XQ} = \log\left(\sum_{x=1}^n p_x |x\rangle \langle x|\otimes\rho_x\right)
= \sum_{x=1}^n |x\rangle \langle x| \otimes \log\left(p_x\rho_x\right)
= \sum_{x=1}^n \log p_x |x\rangle \langle x| \otimes I^Q + \sum_{x=1}^n |x\rangle \langle x| \otimes \log\rho_x,</math>
where <math>I^Q</math> is the identity operator on the quantum system <math>Q</math>. Then, the right-hand side is
:<math>\begin{aligned}
S(X:Q) &= S(X)+S(Q)-S(XQ) \\
&= S(X) + S(\rho) + \operatorname{tr}\left(\rho^{XQ}\log\rho^{XQ}\right) \\
&= S(X) + S(\rho) + \operatorname{tr}\left(\sum_{x=1}^n p_x\log p_x |x\rangle \langle x| \otimes \rho_x\right) + \operatorname{tr}\left(\sum_{x=1}^n p_x|x\rangle \langle x| \otimes \rho_x\log\rho_x\right)\\
&= S(X) + S(\rho) + \underbrace{\operatorname{tr}\left(\sum_{x=1}^n p_x\log p_x |x\rangle \langle x|\right)}_{-S(X)} + \operatorname{tr}\left(\sum_{x=1}^n p_x \rho_x\log\rho_x\right)\\
&= S(\rho) + \sum_{x=1}^n p_x \underbrace{\operatorname{tr}\left(\rho_x\log\rho_x\right)}_{-S(\rho_x)} \\
&= S(\rho) - \sum_{x=1}^n p_x S(\rho_x),
\end{aligned}</math>
which completes the proof.

==Comments and remarks==

In essence, the Holevo bound proves that given ''n'' [[qubit]]s, although they can "carry" a larger amount of (classical) information (thanks to quantum superposition), the amount of classical information that can be ''retrieved'', i.e. ''accessed'', can be only up to ''n'' classical (non-quantum encoded) [[bit]]s. It was also established, both theoretically and experimentally, that there are computations where quantum bits carry more information through the process of the computation than is possible classically.<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1038/s41567-021-01271-7  | volume = 17| pages =  894–897  | last1 =Maslov| first1 = Dmitri| last2 = Kim| first2 = Jin-Sung| last3 = Bravyi| first3 = Sergey| last4 = Yoder| first4 = Theodore J.| last5 = Sheldon| first5 = Sarah|author5-link=Sarah Sheldon| title = Quantum advantage for computations with limited space| journal = Nature Physics| date = 2021-06-28 | issue = 8| arxiv = 2008.06478| bibcode = 2021NatPh..17..894M| s2cid = 221136153}}</ref>
